questions.e: Subclass objects may be assigned to superclass variables, so a Vehicle variable may hold a Car or a Bicycle. The reverse assignment, a supertype object into a subtype variable, is not allowed.

questions.q: Object variables in Java are described as polymorphic because they can hold objects of:
o: only the exact declared type
any type at all, with no restriction
the declared type, or of supertypes of the declared type
the declared type, or of subtypes of the declared type
questions.e: Object variables in Java are polymorphic: they can hold objects of more than one type, namely the declared type or any of its subtypes.

questions.q: Given 'Vehicle v; Car c = new Car();' which statement is a compile-time error?
o: c = v;
Vehicle v2 = new Car();
c = (Car) v;
v = c;
questions.e: A subtype can be assigned to a supertype variable, so v = c is correct, but a supertype cannot be assigned to a subtype variable, so c = v is a compile-time error. A cast, c = (Car) v, fixes this, but only if the Vehicle really is a Car.

questions.q: Which statement about casting is correct?
o: The object is not changed in any way; a runtime check is made and ClassCastException is thrown if the object is not of that type
The cast is checked only at compile time and never fails at runtime
The object is converted into the target type at runtime
A failed cast silently yields null
questions.e: A cast is an object type in parentheses, used to overcome 'type loss'. The object is not changed in any way; a runtime check ensures the object really is of that type, and a ClassCastException results if it is not. Casting should be used sparingly.

questions.q: Casting is described as a way to overcome:
o: memory loss
data hiding
type loss
precision loss
questions.e: A cast is used to overcome 'type loss', which occurs when an object is held in a variable of a supertype and its more specific type is no longer visible to the compiler.

questions.q: Which class is the ultimate superclass of every Java class?
o: Post
Class
Object
Collection
questions.e: All classes inherit from Object, which is why collections can accept elements of type Object and why all classes are subtypes of Object.

questions.q: Without a type parameter, an ArrayList behaves as though declared with which element type?
o: ArrayList<Post>
ArrayList<Object>
ArrayList<Integer>
ArrayList<String>
questions.e: Without a type parameter, ArrayList<Object> is implied; this is likely to produce an 'unchecked or unsafe operations' warning and makes casts more likely to be needed.

questions.q: What is the effect of supplying a type parameter such as ArrayList<Post>?
o: It limits the degree of polymorphism and makes the collection methods typed
It increases the degree of polymorphism to include all Object subtypes
It prevents subclass objects from being stored
It removes the need for a constructor
questions.e: A type parameter limits the degree of polymorphism; the collection methods are then typed, so casts are usually unnecessary and unchecked-operation warnings are avoided.

questions.q: Why must primitive-type values be wrapped before being stored in a collection?
o: Because collections accept elements of object types, and primitive types are not object types
Because collections store only Strings
Because primitives cannot be compared
Because primitives occupy too much memory
questions.e: Potentially all objects can be entered into collections because collections accept elements of type Object and all classes are subtypes of Object; primitive types are not object types, so their values must be wrapped in objects.

questions.q: Which is the correct wrapper class for the primitive type char?
o: Chr
Char
CharacterType
Character
questions.e: The wrapper for char is Character, for int it is Integer and for float it is Float. There is no simple mechanical mapping rule from a primitive's name to its wrapper's name.

questions.q: Which is the correct wrapper class for the primitive type int?
o: IntegerValue
Number
Int
Integer
questions.e: int maps to Integer, float to Float and char to Character; the mapping is not a simple mechanical rule.

questions.q: In 'markList.add(mark);' where markList is an ArrayList<Integer> and mark is an int, the conversion that takes place is called:
o: autoboxing
overloading
unboxing
casting
questions.e: Autoboxing automatically wraps the primitive int into an Integer on the way into the collection. The reverse, as in 'int firstMark = markList.remove(0);', is unboxing.

questions.q: In 'int firstMark = markList.remove(0);' where markList is an ArrayList<Integer>, the conversion that takes place is called:
o: casting
unboxing
substitution
autoboxing
questions.e: Unboxing automatically extracts the primitive value from the wrapper object; the opposite direction is autoboxing.

questions.q: Explicit wrapping and unwrapping, as in 'Integer iwrap = new Integer(i);' followed by 'int value = iwrap.intValue();' is rarely needed in practice because:
o: autoboxing and unboxing perform these conversions automatically
collections now accept primitive types directly
int and Integer are the same type
the compiler removes all wrapper objects
questions.e: Autoboxing and unboxing mean programmers do not often have to wrap and unwrap values explicitly.

questions.q: When a single superclass type is used for a collection, what does the client's display loop become?
o: A recursive method over the inheritance hierarchy
A single loop such as for(Post post : posts) { post.display(); }
Two loops, one per subclass, as before
A loop containing an explicit cast for each element
questions.e: With one collection of the superclass type, the client needs only one loop, calling display() on each element; the correct subclass behaviour is selected at runtime.

questions.q: An inheritance hierarchy in which a master's student is a student and a student is a person illustrates that:
o: inheritance hierarchies can have more than two levels
inheritance is limited to two levels in Java
subclasses cannot add their own fields
every hierarchy must have exactly one subclass per superclass
questions.e: Such hierarchies are commonplace; when new types are added, the hierarchy may be extended to further levels, and the common attributes do not need to be rewritten.

questions.q: Why are computer simulations typically only partial?
o: Programming languages cannot express complete models
Complete simulations are forbidden by scientific convention
They involve simplifications, because greater detail requires more processing power, memory and simulation time
Partial simulations are more accurate than complete ones
questions.e: Simulations are typically only partial, tackling and revealing part of the story. They usually involve simplifications, or models; greater detail has the potential to provide greater accuracy but typically requires more processing power, memory and simulation time.

questions.q: Which benefit of simulation allows questions such as 'how will wildlife be affected if a highway is cut through this national park?' to be investigated?
o: They allow experimentation that is safer, cheaper and quicker
They model phenomena with complete accuracy
They guarantee that the predicted outcome will occur
They remove the need for any real-world measurement
questions.e: Simulations help us understand, optimize and predict; they support useful prediction, such as the weather, and allow experimentation that is safer, cheaper and quicker than the real thing.

questions.q: A predator-prey simulation is a standard scenario in which field?
o: Fluid dynamics
Numerical analysis
Population dynamics
Queueing theory
questions.e: Predator-prey simulations are a standard scenario in population dynamics, where there is often a delicate balance between species: more prey means more food, more food encourages higher predator numbers, more predators eat more prey, and so on.

questions.q: In a foxes-and-rabbits simulation, which class creates the initial state, manages the overall simulation task and holds the collection of animals?
o: Field
Simulator
Location
SimulatorView
questions.e: Simulator creates the simulation's initial state, manages the overall simulation task by performing a sequence of steps in which each animal is allowed to move, and holds a collection of foxes and rabbits; it plays the role of the 'main program'.

questions.q: In that simulation, which class represents a two-dimensional enclosed area with positions arranged in a matrix?
o: Location
Counter
FieldStats
Field
questions.e: Field represents a 2D enclosed field with positions arranged matrix-style, while Location represents a single 2D position and can hold at most one animal.

questions.q: How many animals can a single Location hold?
o: At most two
At most one
Exactly one
Any number
questions.e: Location represents a 2D position and can hold one animal at most, so a position may also be empty.

questions.q: Which classes in the simulation maintain statistics and present a view of the field, and have nothing to do with the model itself?
o: Actor, Drawable and Animal
SimulatorView, FieldStats and Counter
Field, Location and Simulator
Fox, Rabbit and Animal
questions.e: SimulatorView, FieldStats and Counter maintain statistics and present a view of the field; they are separate from the model.

questions.q: In a Rabbit class, which of these is an instance field rather than a property shared by all rabbits?
o: The breeding age
The rabbit's current age
The maximum age
The breeding probability
questions.e: Individual characteristics such as age, alive and location are instance fields. Properties valid for all rabbits, such as breeding age, maximum age, breeding probability and maximum litter size, are held in static fields.

questions.q: Which method manages a rabbit's behaviour, and which manages a fox's?
o: hunt for the rabbit and run for the fox
act for the rabbit and run for the fox
run for the rabbit and hunt for the fox
move for the rabbit and eat for the fox
questions.e: A rabbit's behaviour is managed from its run method and a fox's from its hunt method. When a common superclass is introduced, both are renamed act.

questions.q: Which simplification applies to the rabbits in the simulation?
o: Rabbits are created only at the start of the simulation
Rabbits move only in a single fixed direction
Rabbits never breed and never die
Rabbits do not have different genders, and all rabbits die at the same age
questions.e: The simplifications are that rabbits do not have different genders, that the same rabbit could breed at every step, and that all rabbits die at the same age.

questions.q: What extra field does a Fox have that a Rabbit does not?
o: age
location
foodLevel
alive
questions.e: A fox has age, alive and location like a rabbit, plus foodLevel, which is increased by eating rabbits.

questions.q: What happens when a fox finds a rabbit in an adjacent location?
o: The fox's food level is decreased and the rabbit flees
The rabbit is killed and the fox's food level is increased
A new fox is born at that location
Both animals are removed from the field
questions.e: Foxes get hungry and hunt for food in adjacent locations; if a fox finds a rabbit in an adjacent location, the rabbit is killed and the fox's food level is increased.

questions.q: Which are the three key components of the Simulator class?
o: The run method, the hunt method, and the act method
Setup in the constructor, the populate method, and the simulateOneStep method
The constructor, the destructor, and the main method
The field, the view, and the statistics
questions.e: The three key components are setup of the simulation in the constructor, the populate method in which each animal is given a random starting age, and the simulateOneStep method, which iterates over the population using two Field objects, field and updatedField.

questions.q: In a single simulation step, how many Field objects are used?
o: One, which is modified in place
Two: the current field and an updated field
One per animal
Three: current, updated and previous
questions.e: The simulateOneStep method iterates over the population and uses two Field objects: field and updatedField.

questions.q: The Java operator instanceof is used to:
o: convert an object from one class to another
compare two objects for equality of contents
check whether a given object is an instance of a given class
create a new instance of a class
questions.e: instanceof checks whether a given object is an instance of a given class; it appears in code such as 'if(animal instanceof Rabbit) { Rabbit rabbit = (Rabbit)animal; ... }'.

questions.q: Code that tests each animal with instanceof and then casts it before calling run or hunt reveals which design weaknesses?
o: The animals have too much shared implementation
Fox and Rabbit have strong similarities but no common superclass, and the Simulator is tightly coupled to the specific classes
The Simulator has too few responsibilities
Fox and Rabbit are too loosely coupled to each other
questions.e: Fox and Rabbit have strong similarities yet do not share a superclass, and the Simulator 'knows' a lot about the behaviour of foxes and rabbits, so it is tightly coupled to those specific classes.

questions.q: When an Animal superclass is introduced, which fields move into it?
o: age, alive and foodLevel
location and foodLevel only
username, timestamp and likes
age, alive and location
questions.e: The common fields age, alive and location are placed in Animal, and the methods run and hunt are renamed act so that polymorphic method calls can replace the instanceof tests.

questions.q: Renaming run and hunt to a single method name act supports which goal?
o: Allowing Animal to be instantiated directly
Information hiding, through polymorphic method calls that decouple the Simulator
Faster execution of each simulation step
Reducing the number of fields in Animal
questions.e: Method renaming to a single name supports information hiding via polymorphic method calls, so the Simulator can be significantly decoupled: it deals with animals rather than with rabbits and foxes.

questions.q: Why must act be declared abstract in the Animal class rather than given a body?
o: An abstract method cannot be overridden, which guarantees correctness
Abstract methods execute faster than concrete ones
Static type checking requires the method to exist in Animal, but there is no obvious shared implementation
Java forbids concrete methods in superclasses
questions.e: Static type checking requires an act method in Animal even though it will never be executed, and there is no obvious shared implementation, since either run or hunt should run and nothing else. So act is declared abstract.

questions.q: Which three properties characterise an abstract method?
o: It is private, has no body, and may be instantiated
It has abstract in its signature, it has no body, and it makes its class abstract
It has abstract in its signature, it has a body, and its class stays concrete
It has no signature, has a body, and must be static
questions.e: Abstract methods have abstract in the signature, have no body, and make the class abstract.

questions.q: Which statement about abstract classes is correct?
o: They can be instantiated but cannot be subclassed
They must declare all of their fields as abstract
They may contain only abstract methods and no concrete ones
They cannot be instantiated and they are the only classes that may contain abstract methods
questions.e: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and are the only classes with abstract methods. They function as incomplete superclasses, and they support polymorphism.

questions.q: What obligation does a concrete subclass of an abstract class have?
o: It must not override any inherited method
It must provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods
It must be declared final
It must declare at least one new abstract method
questions.e: Concrete subclasses complete the implementation, which means they must provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods.

questions.q: Multiple inheritance means:
o: having a class inherit directly from multiple ancestors
having a class contain fields of several other classes
having a class implement several methods of the same name
having several classes inherit from one ancestor
questions.e: Multiple inheritance is having a class inherit directly from multiple ancestors; the subclass then has all the features of all superclasses plus those defined in itself. Each language has its own rules for resolving competing definitions.

questions.q: What is Java's position on multiple inheritance?
o: Java permits it for both classes and interfaces
Java forbids it for both classes and interfaces
Java forbids it for classes but permits it for interfaces
Java permits it for classes but forbids it for interfaces
questions.e: Java forbids multiple inheritance for classes and permits it for interfaces, because interfaces carry no competing implementation.

questions.q: Which set of properties describes a Java interface?
o: The keyword interface instead of class, concrete methods with bodies, and private fields
The keyword abstract instead of class, one constructor, and protected fields
The keyword interface instead of class, abstract methods only with no constructors, and public method signatures with constant fields only
The keyword implements instead of class, no methods, and no fields
questions.e: An interface uses the keyword interface instead of class, declares abstract methods only and no constructors, and may contain only public method signatures and constant fields.

questions.q: An interface is most similar to:
o: a generic collection class
an enumerated type
a concrete class containing no fields
an abstract class containing abstract methods only
questions.e: Interfaces look similar to classes at first glance but do not include method bodies, so they are similar to abstract classes with abstract methods only; interfaces are fully abstract.

questions.q: Which declaration is correct for a class that inherits implementation from Animal and also conforms to the Drawable interface?
o: public class Fox extends Animal implements Drawable
public class Fox implements Animal, Drawable
public class Fox implements Animal extends Drawable
public class Fox extends Animal, Drawable
questions.e: extends is used for class inheritance and implements for interface inheritance; a class may extend at most one class but implement any number of interfaces.

questions.q: A class may extend how many classes and implement how many interfaces?
o: Extend any number of classes, implement any number of interfaces
Extend at most one class, implement any number of interfaces
Extend any number of classes, implement at most one interface
Extend at most one class, implement at most one interface
questions.e: Extend at most one class, implement any number of interfaces.

questions.q: Given 'public class Hunter implements Actor, Drawable', what can be concluded?
o: Hunter inherits method bodies from both Actor and Drawable
Hunter inherits no implementation from Actor or Drawable but is a subtype of both
Hunter must be declared abstract
Hunter cannot be stored in a collection of Actor
questions.e: Implementing classes do not inherit code, but they are subtypes of the interface type, so polymorphism is available with interfaces as well as with classes.

questions.q: If an Animal class contains concrete methods with bodies, what follows?
o: Animal must be converted into an interface
Animal must stay a class and cannot be converted into an interface
Animal cannot have any abstract methods
Animal must be declared final
questions.e: Animal stays a class precisely because it contains concrete methods with bodies; interfaces cannot carry method bodies.

questions.q: What is the main gain from using an interface, given that no code is inherited from it?
o: Implementing classes need no constructors
Implementing classes automatically gain fields
Implementing classes execute faster
Implementing classes become subtypes of the interface type, so polymorphism is available
questions.e: Implementing classes do not inherit code, but they are subtypes of the interface type, so polymorphism works with interfaces just as it does with classes.

questions.q: Interfaces as specifications give a strong separation of functionality from implementation, with the qualification that:
o: clients must know which implementation they are using
the number of implementing classes is limited to one
parameter and return types are still mandated
method names are still mandated but types are not
questions.e: Interfaces provide a strong separation of functionality from implementation, though parameter and return types are mandated. Clients interact independently of the implementation but can choose from alternative implementations.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches the two kinds of thing inheritance provides with the constructs that provide them?
o: Shared implementation from interfaces; shared type information from abstract classes only
Shared implementation from enums; shared type information from collections
Shared implementation and shared type information both only from concrete classes
Shared implementation from concrete and abstract classes; shared type information from classes and interfaces
questions.e: Inheritance can provide shared implementation, through concrete and abstract classes, and it provides shared type information, through both classes and interfaces.

questions.q: Abstract methods are valuable because they allow:
o: multiple inheritance of implementation
instantiation of incomplete objects
runtime type checking without requiring a declaration
static type checking without requiring an implementation
questions.e: Abstract methods allow static type checking without requiring implementation; abstract classes function as incomplete superclasses with no instances, and they support polymorphism.

questions.q: Prototyping is defined as the activity of:
o: writing the final production code in short increments
testing a finished product with a sample of users
producing an interactive version of design ideas so users can effectively evaluate the design of an interactive product
documenting requirements in a formal notation
questions.e: For users to effectively evaluate the design of an interactive product, designers must produce an interactive version of their ideas; this activity is called prototyping.

questions.q: In design fields outside interaction design, a prototype is typically:
o: a cost estimate for manufacturing
a full-size working copy of the product
a written specification of the product
a small-scale model, such as a miniature car or a model of a building
questions.e: In other design fields a prototype is a small-scale model, such as a miniature car or a model of a building. In interaction design it may be screen sketches, a slide show, a video, a lump of wood, a cardboard mock-up or software with limited functionality.

questions.q: Which of the following can serve as a prototype in interaction design?
o: A project Gantt chart
A cardboard mock-up
A signed requirements document
A completed user manual
questions.e: Prototypes in interaction design include a series of screen sketches, a slide show, a video simulating the use of a system, a lump of wood standing in for a hand-held computer, a cardboard mock-up, and a piece of software with limited functionality.

questions.q: Which reason for prototyping is concerned with clarifying vague requirements?
o: Validation of design ideas
Communication among team members
Choosing between alternatives
Evaluation and feedback
questions.e: The four reasons are evaluation and feedback, communication among team members (which clarifies vague requirements), validation of design ideas (testing technical feasibility), and choosing between alternatives.

questions.q: Which reason for prototyping is concerned with testing the technical feasibility of an idea?
o: Communication among team members
Validation of design ideas
Evaluation and feedback
Choosing between alternatives
questions.e: Validation of design ideas means testing out the technical feasibility of an idea; evaluation and feedback lets stakeholders interact with an envisioned product in realistic settings.

questions.q: Which of the following should be prototyped?
o: Only the final visual styling
Difficult, controversial or critical areas
Only areas that are already well understood
Only the database schema
questions.e: What to prototype: technical issues; workflow and task design; screen layouts and information display; and difficult, controversial or critical areas.

questions.q: A low-fidelity prototype is characterised by the fact that it:
o: is built with the same development tools as the final product
is sketchy and incomplete and uses materials very different from the intended final version
is always evolved into the final system
closely resembles the final product in details and functionality
questions.e: A low-fidelity prototype is sketchy and incomplete, does not look very much like the final product, and uses materials such as paper and cardboard rather than electronic screens and metal.

questions.q: At which stage of development are low-fidelity prototypes used, and why?
o: Late stages, because they are the most accurate representation
Early stages, because they are cheap and easy to modify, supporting exploration of alternatives
Throughout, because they are integrated into the final system
Only after high-fidelity prototypes have been evaluated
questions.e: Low-fidelity prototypes are used during early stages of development because they are cheap and easy to modify, so they support the exploration of alternative designs and ideas.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a low-fidelity prototype and the final system?
o: It is never intended to be integrated into the final system; it is for exploration only
It replaces the need for a final system
It must be preserved as the system's documentation
It always becomes the first version of the final system
questions.e: A low-fidelity prototype is never intended to be integrated into the final system; such prototypes are for exploration only.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of low-fidelity prototyping?
o: Smalltalk
Macromedia Director
Index cards
Visual Basic
questions.e: Examples of low-fidelity prototyping are storyboards, sketching, index cards and the 'Wizard of Oz' technique. Macromedia Director, Visual Basic, Smalltalk and web development tools are common high-fidelity development environments.

questions.q: Storyboards, a prototyping technique borrowed from film, consist of:
o: snapshots of the interface at particular points in the interaction, as a series of sketches
working software with limited functionality
a single detailed drawing of the final screen layout
written scripts with no visual content
questions.e: A storyboard is a series of sketches giving snapshots of the interface at particular points in the interaction, showing how a user can perform a task using the device. Storyboards are often used with scenarios and let stakeholders role play by stepping through the scenario.

questions.q: Storyboards are often used together with which other technique, to which they add visual detail?
o: Scenarios
Style guides
Class diagrams
Unit tests
questions.e: Storyboards are often used with scenarios, bringing more detail to the written scenario and offering stakeholders a chance to role play with the prototype.

questions.q: In sketching as a prototyping technique, which statement is correct?
o: Only flowcharts may be used, never block diagrams
Sketches must be produced with a computer drawing tool
Professional drawing skills are essential for the sketches to be useful
Drawing skills are not critical; symbols indicate tasks, activities and objects
questions.e: Drawing skills are not critical: symbols indicate tasks, activities and objects, flowcharts handle time-related issues, and block diagrams show functional components.

questions.q: In sketching, which notation is suggested for time-related issues?
o: Index cards
Block diagrams
Flowcharts
Storyboards
questions.e: Flowcharts are used for time-related issues, while block diagrams are used for functional components.

questions.q: In index-card prototyping, what does each card represent and what size are the cards?
o: One screen, on cards of 3 by 5 inches
One class, on cards of 3 by 5 inches
One scenario, on cards of 4 by 6 inches
One user task, on cards of 5 by 8 inches
questions.e: Index cards are small cards of 3 by 5 inches, each representing one screen; multiple screens can be shown easily on a table or wall, and thread or lines indicate relationships such as sequence and hyperlinks.

questions.q: Index-card prototyping is particularly associated with which kind of development?
o: Database administration
Website development
Compiler construction
Embedded firmware development
questions.e: Index cards are often used in website development, where threads or lines between cards can indicate sequence and hyperlinks between screens.

questions.q: In 'Wizard of Oz' prototyping, the user:
o: writes the responses that the system will later produce
interacts only with paper mock-ups
is told in advance that a human will generate all responses
interacts with an interface without knowing that the responses are generated by a human rather than a computer
questions.e: A Wizard of Oz prototype works by having someone behind the scenes pulling the levers; the user interacts with the interface without knowing that the responses are being generated by a human, not a computer. This allows difficult interface concepts to be tested before a system is fully working.

questions.q: A high-fidelity prototype is defined as:
o: a written specification of the product's behaviour
a paper-based representation produced in the earliest design stages
the released product itself
a computer-based interactive representation of the product in its closest resemblance to the final design in details and functionality
questions.e: A high-fidelity prototype is a computer-based interactive representation of the product in its closest resemblance to the final design in terms of details and functionality.

questions.q: High-fidelity prototypes cover which two aspects of the product?
o: The database schema and the network protocol
The user interface in terms of visuals and aesthetics, and the user experience in terms of interactions, user flow and behaviour
The project schedule and the cost model
The source code structure and the build process
questions.e: High-fidelity prototypes cover not only the user interface in terms of visuals and aesthetics, but also user experience aspects in terms of interactions, user flow and behaviour.

questions.q: A high-fidelity prototype looks more like the final system in terms of:
o: both appearance and functionality equally
functionality, not appearance
neither appearance nor functionality
appearance, not functionality
questions.e: With materials and methods similar or identical to those of the final product, a high-fidelity prototype looks more like the final system in appearance, not functionality.

questions.q: What is the risk of 'misled user expectations' in high-fidelity prototyping?
o: Users may expect the product to be cheaper
Developers may underestimate the schedule
Users may refuse to engage with the prototype
Users may think they have a full system
questions.e: Because a high-fidelity prototype closely resembles the final product, users may think they have a full system when in fact functionality is limited.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a low-fidelity prototype?
o: A clearly defined navigational scheme
Fully interactive behaviour
Low developmental cost and the ability to evaluate multiple design concepts
The look and feel of the final product
questions.e: Low-fidelity prototypes offer low developmental cost and allow multiple design concepts to be evaluated; their disadvantages are limited error checking and navigational and flow limitations.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of a low-fidelity prototype?
o: Long build time
Limited error checking, with navigational and flow limitations
High development cost
Developer reluctance to change crafted work
questions.e: Low-fidelity prototypes suffer from limited error checking and navigational and flow limitations; expense, build time and developer reluctance to change crafted work are disadvantages of high-fidelity prototypes.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a high-fidelity prototype?
o: It is quick to build
It is fully interactive and clearly defines the navigational scheme
It is easy for developers to discard
It has a low developmental cost
questions.e: High-fidelity prototypes are fully interactive, give the look and feel of the final product, and clearly define the navigational scheme.

questions.q: Which human factor counts as a disadvantage of high-fidelity prototypes?
o: Users refuse to evaluate polished interfaces
Managers will not fund the evaluation
Designers cannot agree on colour schemes
Developers are reluctant to change something they have crafted for hours
questions.e: Alongside being more expensive to develop and time consuming to build, high-fidelity prototypes suffer because developers are reluctant to change something they have crafted for hours.

questions.q: A compromise that provides a wide range of functions but with little detail is called:
o: horizontal
shallow-deep
evolutionary
vertical
questions.e: The two common types of compromise are 'horizontal', which provides a wide range of functions with little detail, and 'vertical', which provides a lot of detail for only a few functions.

questions.q: A compromise that provides a lot of detail for only a few functions is called:
o: vertical
throw-away
horizontal
evolutionary
questions.e: A vertical, or deep, compromise provides a lot of detail for only a few functions; a horizontal, or shallow, compromise provides a wide range of functions with little detail.

questions.q: Which compromise is characteristic of a low-fidelity prototype?
o: The icons are sketchy
The device doesn't actually work
The response is slow
Only limited functionality is available
questions.e: All prototypes involve compromises. For a low-fidelity prototype the compromise is that the device doesn't actually work; for a high-fidelity prototype the compromises are slow response, sketchy icons and limited functionality.

questions.q: Which development philosophy involves evolving a prototype into the final product?
o: Horizontal prototyping
Wizard of Oz prototyping
Evolutionary prototyping
Throw-away prototyping
questions.e: Evolutionary prototyping involves evolving a prototype into the final product; throw-away prototyping uses the prototype as a stepping stone, after which it is discarded and the final system is built from scratch.

questions.q: In throw-away prototyping, what happens after the prototype has served its purpose?
o: The prototype becomes the system's test harness
The prototype is thrown away and the final system is built from scratch
The prototype is shipped as the first release
The prototype is refined incrementally into the final system
questions.e: Throw-away prototyping uses the prototype as a stepping stone towards the final design; the prototype is thrown away and the final system is built from scratch.

questions.q: Even after extensive user evaluation of prototypes, the final product must still be subjected to rigorous quality testing for:
o: coupling, cohesion, fan-in and fan-out
cost, schedule, staffing and scope
colour, typography, spacing and iconography
reliability, robustness, maintainability, integrity, portability and efficiency
questions.e: Although prototypes have undergone extensive user evaluation, the final product still has to be subjected to rigorous quality testing for reliability, robustness, maintainability, integrity, portability and efficiency.

questions.q: Conceptual design is defined as a description of the proposed system in terms of:
o: the hardware platform and deployment architecture
a set of integrated ideas and concepts about what it should do, behave and look like, understandable by users in the manner intended
the concrete widgets, menus and icons that make up the interface
the classes, fields and methods that implement the system
questions.e: Conceptual design is a description of the proposed system in terms of a set of integrated ideas and concepts about what it should do, behave and look like, that will be understandable by the users in the manner intended. Physical design covers the concrete interface details.

questions.q: Which design objective corresponds to identifying the critical interaction aspects of a product?
o: Conceptual design
Physical design
Scenario writing
Prototyping
questions.e: Identifying critical interaction aspects is conceptual design; selecting appropriate tools and methods to provide interactivity is physical design.

questions.q: Conceptual design transforms user requirements and needs into:
o: a physical screen layout, in a single pass
a conceptual model, through stepwise refinement and consideration of alternatives
a test plan, through requirements tracing
source code, through automated generation
questions.e: Conceptual design is the transformation of user requirements and needs into a conceptual model, by stepwise refinement, with consideration of alternatives via prototyping and scenarios.

questions.q: Which three perspectives are used for developing a conceptual model?
o: Menu design, icon design and screen design
Low fidelity, high fidelity and evolutionary
Interaction mode, metaphor and interaction paradigm
Reliability, portability and efficiency
questions.e: The three perspectives for developing a conceptual model are interaction mode, metaphor and interaction paradigm.

questions.q: Which of these is an activity-based interaction mode?
o: Exploring and browsing
Product-oriented
Process-oriented
Object-based
questions.e: The activity-based interaction modes are instructing, conversing, manipulating and navigating, and exploring and browsing. Object-based is the alternative to activity-based, while process-oriented and product-oriented describe a different axis.

questions.q: A telephone menu that says 'Press 1 for customer service' exemplifies which interaction mode?
o: Manipulating and navigating
Conversing
Exploring and browsing
Instructing
questions.e: A phone menu is the example given for conversing; computer-aided design exemplifies instructing, the desktop exemplifies manipulating, and DVDs exemplify exploring.

questions.q: A desktop interface, in which users drag and arrange items directly, exemplifies which interaction mode?
o: Manipulating and navigating
Instructing
Conversing
Object-based
questions.e: The desktop is the example of manipulating and navigating; a phone menu illustrates conversing and a computer-aided design tool illustrates instructing.

questions.q: Software that supports work processes, such as financial software, is described as:
o: activity-based
process-oriented
product-oriented
object-based
questions.e: Process-oriented software supports work processes, such as financial software; product-oriented software develops products that users create, modify and maintain, such as a spreadsheet or word processor.

questions.q: Software in which users create, modify and maintain products, such as a spreadsheet or word processor, is described as:
o: conversing
instructing
process-oriented
product-oriented
questions.e: Product-oriented applications let users create, modify and maintain products; process-oriented applications support work processes such as financial workflows.

questions.q: A conceptual model based on objects users already know gives them:
o: an exact replica of the familiar object's behaviour
a complete specification of the product's internals
a guarantee that no new features will be added
clues about what the product does and does not support
questions.e: Conceptual models based on familiar objects provide users with clues about what a product does and does not support, and often give a good starting point for exploring a new product. Typically the new product will have additional features compared with the object it is based on.

questions.q: An interface metaphor is best described as:
o: a partial mapping of the software to a real object, combining familiar knowledge with new knowledge
a formal specification of the interface's behaviour
a visual theme applied to the interface after the design is finished
a complete mapping of the software to a real object, with identical behaviour
questions.e: Interface metaphors are a partial mapping of the software to a real object; they combine familiar knowledge with new knowledge and help the user understand the product. Metaphors are meant to hint at the essence of a product or process.

questions.q: What are the three steps for choosing a good metaphor, in order?
o: Generate metaphors, test them with users, select the most popular
Identify critical areas, build a prototype, evaluate the metaphor
Generate metaphors, understand system functionality, discard unsuitable ones
Understand system functionality, identify potential problem or critical areas, generate metaphors
questions.e: The three-step process is: understand system functionality, identify potential problem or complicated and critical areas, and generate metaphors.

questions.q: Programs that autonomously explore the World Wide Web by following links, used by search engines to index pages, are called 'spiders'. This naming illustrates:
o: an interface metaphor, since the systems follow links as a spider follows the threads of its web
a design pattern, since it names a reusable code structure
a scenario, since it describes an imagined situation
an interaction paradigm, since it defines a coherent set of interaction methods
questions.e: The metaphor is that these systems are like spiders following the threads that make up their web; one does not have to understand the details to get a sense of what they do.

questions.q: Which question belongs to the evaluation of a metaphor?
o: How many lines of code will it take to implement?
How many screens will it require?
How extensible is it, that is, are there extra aspects useful later on?
Which programming language best supports it?
questions.e: A metaphor is evaluated by how much structure it provides, how relevant it is to the problem, whether it is easy to represent, whether the audience will understand it, and how extensible it is.

questions.q: Why does relevance matter when evaluating a metaphor?
o: A relevant metaphor requires no user testing
A relevant metaphor reduces confusion and false expectations
A relevant metaphor is cheaper to illustrate
A relevant metaphor guarantees extensibility
questions.e: Relevance to the problem matters because it reduces confusion and false expectations; a metaphor also requires a sound and familiar structure.

questions.q: Interface metaphors are popular mainly because:
o: they remove the need for any documentation
they are required by most style guides
they explain difficult concepts in terms of something familiar, where computer systems often have no direct real-world analog
they make the software run faster
questions.e: Interface metaphors can help explain difficult concepts sufficiently in terms of something that is familiar; computer systems are often complex and have no direct analog in the real world, so metaphors explain them without lots of technical detail.

questions.q: An interaction paradigm is defined as:
o: a coherent collection of interaction methods that addresses environmental requirements
a concrete arrangement of widgets on a screen
the mode by which a user invokes actions
a partial mapping of software onto a familiar object
questions.e: An interaction paradigm is a coherent collection of interaction methods addressing environmental requirements; examples include the desktop paradigm, ubiquitous computing, pervasive computing, wearable computing and mobile devices.

questions.q: In the desktop paradigm, what does the abbreviation WIMP stand for?
o: Windows, icons, menus and pointers
Windows, interfaces, modes and pointers
Workspaces, icons, menus and palettes
Widgets, images, menus and panels
questions.e: The desktop paradigm is the WIMP interface: windows, icons, menus and pointers.

questions.q: Which of the following is an interaction paradigm?
o: Wearable computing
Instructing
Storyboarding
Metaphor
questions.e: Interaction paradigms include the desktop paradigm, ubiquitous computing, pervasive computing, wearable computing and mobile devices. Instructing is an interaction mode, and metaphor is a separate perspective on the conceptual model.

questions.q: When expanding a conceptual model, functions may be related to each other temporally or by:
o: delegation
concatenation
inheritance
categorization
questions.e: Expanding the conceptual model asks what functions the product will perform, how the functions are related to each other (temporally, that is sequentially or in parallel, or by categorization), and what information needs to be available.

questions.q: Scenarios are used in the design process to:
o: measure the system's runtime performance
serve as scripts for user evaluation of prototypes and as concrete examples of tasks
define the project's budget and schedule
specify the system's class structure
questions.e: Scenarios express proposed or imagined situations and are used as scripts for user evaluation of prototypes, as concrete examples of tasks, as a means of co-operation across professional boundaries, and to sell ideas to users and potential customers.

questions.q: 'Plus' and 'minus' scenarios are used for:
o: comparing two development philosophies
measuring user satisfaction scores
exploration of extreme cases
recording positive and negative user feedback
questions.e: Plus and minus scenarios support the exploration of extreme cases.

questions.q: Continuous prototyping during conceptual design means using:
o: only low-fidelity prototypes throughout
high-fidelity prototypes early on and low-fidelity prototypes later
only high-fidelity prototypes throughout
low-fidelity prototypes early on and high-fidelity prototypes later
questions.e: Continuous prototyping uses low-fidelity prototypes early on and high-fidelity prototypes later; under evolutionary prototyping, early prototypes are gradually enhanced and augmented in appearance and functionality.

questions.q: Physical design is concerned with:
o: the choice of development philosophy
the identification of critical interaction aspects
the concrete, detailed issues of designing the interface
the integrated set of ideas about what the system should do
questions.e: Physical design covers the concrete, detailed issues of designing the interface; the term is also used, although inaccurately, for software-based systems.

questions.q: Which of these is a named source of guidelines for physical design?
o: Fowler's refactoring catalogue
McConnell's construction fundamentals
Constantine's factoring rules
Shneiderman's eight golden rules
questions.e: Guidelines for physical design include Nielsen's heuristics, Shneiderman's eight golden rules, and style guides used for commercial or corporate purposes.

questions.q: A style guide is best described as:
o: a list of widgets available in a development toolkit
a record of user complaints about an interface
a set of usability heuristics published by an individual researcher
a collection of design rules and principles that decides the 'look and feel'
questions.e: Style guides serve commercial or corporate purposes and are a collection of design rules and principles that decide the 'look and feel'.

questions.q: Which four areas of emphasis make up physical design for computer interaction?
o: Storyboards, sketching, index cards and Wizard of Oz
Interaction mode, metaphor, paradigm and scenario
Reliability, robustness, portability and efficiency
Menu design, icon design, screen design and information display
questions.e: The emphasis in physical design falls on menu design, icon design, screen design and information display, using widgets such as dialog boxes, toolbars, icons and menus.

questions.q: In menu design, 'arrangement' covers which concerns?
o: Screen size and input method
Sub-menus and dialog boxes
The number of menus, their length and the order of items
Categorization and visual division by colours and dividing lines
questions.e: Arrangement covers the number of menus, length and order of items; grouping covers categorization and visual division; structure covers sub-menus and dialog boxes; and constraints cover screen size and input method.

questions.q: In menu design, screen size and input method are classed as:
o: arrangement
grouping
constraints
terminology
questions.e: Constraints in menu design are screen size and input method; context concerns the applicability of entries.

questions.q: Which practical tip applies to icon design?
o: Icons should avoid existing traditions and standards to stay original
Icons need not be distinguishable from one another if labelled
Concrete objects or things are easier to represent than actions
Actions are easier to represent than concrete objects
questions.e: Good icon design is difficult: an icon has to be widely acceptable, its meaning readily perceivable and distinguishable from others. The tips are to always draw on existing traditions or standards, and that concrete objects or things are easier to represent than actions.

questions.q: The meaning of an icon is described as:
o: irrelevant if a tooltip is provided
universal across all users
determined solely by its colour
cultural and context sensitive
questions.e: The meaning of icons is cultural and context sensitive, which is why an icon has to be widely acceptable and its meaning readily perceivable.

questions.q: When splitting functions across screens, the starting point is:
o: the database schema, with each screen matching one table
task analysis, with each screen containing a single simple step
the style guide, with each screen matching one template
the class diagram, with each screen matching one class
questions.e: Task analysis is the starting point; each screen should contain a single simple step, though too many simple screens causes user frustration. Context requires all pertinent information to be available at relevant times.

questions.q: What is the risk of making each screen contain only a single simple step?
o: Navigation becomes impossible
The screens become overcrowded
Context information is duplicated
Too many simple screens causes user frustration
questions.e: Each screen should contain a single simple step, but too many simple screens leads to user frustration; context requires that all pertinent information be available at relevant times, which may mean multiple screens open at once.

questions.q: In individual screen design, animation is characterised as:
o: always preferable to colour for directing attention
very powerful but potentially distracting
the only reliable way to group items
ineffective at directing user attention
questions.e: User attention is directed to the salient point by means such as colour and motion; animation is very powerful but can be distracting.

questions.q: Which means of grouping items on a screen is identified in physical design?
o: Timing of appearance only
Font size only
Physical proximity, colour and shape
Alphabetical ordering only
questions.e: Grouping uses physical proximity, colour and shape; structure provides connections between related items, and there is a trade-off between sparse population and overcrowding.

questions.q: In individual screen design, the trade-off to be managed is between:
o: sparse population and overcrowding
animation and static layout
colour and monochrome
menus and toolbars
questions.e: The trade-off is sparse population versus overcrowding; the balance between information or interaction and clarity is the same concern.

questions.q: Which types of information display are distinguished when designing information display?
o: Alpha-numerical, chart and graphs
Textual, audio and haptic
Primary, secondary and tertiary
Static, dynamic and interactive
questions.e: Different types of information imply different kinds of display: alpha-numerical, chart and graphs. Context requires relevant information to be available at all times in the most efficient format for the task.

questions.q: In information display, consistency is required between:
o: the prototype and the project schedule
the icon set and the menu structure
paper display and screen data entry, and between different screens showing similar information
the development environment and the deployment platform
questions.e: Consistency applies between paper display and screen data entry, and between different screens with similar information, which may be customisable; information content is distinguished from presentation.

questions.q: Refactoring is defined as:
o: changing the structure of code without changing its functionality
adding new features while improving performance
changing the functionality of code without changing its structure
rewriting code in a different programming language
questions.e: Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its functionality.

questions.q: Martin Fowler defines refactoring as a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify:
o: by rewriting it from scratch
without any need for testing
while extending its observable behavior
without changing its observable behavior
questions.e: Fowler's definition is 'a change made to the internal structure of the software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior'.

questions.q: Fowler describes the essence of refactoring as applying a series of small behavior-preserving transformations, each of which is:
o: individually significant but collectively negligible
too small to be worth doing on its own, though the cumulative effect is significant
provably optimal in isolation
large enough to require a separate release
questions.e: Fowler calls refactoring a controlled technique for improving the design of an existing code base, whose essence is applying a series of small behavior-preserving transformations, each 'too small to be worth doing', whose cumulative effect is quite significant.

questions.q: The word 'refactoring' in modern programming grew out of whose original use of the word 'factoring' in structured programming?
o: Larry Constantine
Bertrand Meyer
Martin Fowler
Steve McConnell
questions.e: Refactoring grew out of Larry Constantine's original use of the word 'factoring' in structured programming, which referred to decomposing a program into its constituent parts as much as possible.

questions.q: In structured programming, 'factoring' referred to:
o: dividing a team into specialised roles
extracting common subexpressions for speed
decomposing a program into its constituent parts as much as possible
combining several programs into a single executable
questions.e: Larry Constantine's 'factoring' referred to decomposing a program into its constituent parts as much as possible.

questions.q: Code that requires refactoring is said to have:
o: a bug
a fault
a smell
a leak
questions.e: When code requires refactoring, it is said to have a 'smell' - not literally, but such code does not look very appealing.

questions.q: Why does a large class tend to keep growing?
o: Coding standards usually require few classes
Large classes execute faster than small ones
It is usually easier for a developer to add a feature to an existing class than to create a new one
Compilers merge small classes automatically
questions.e: A large class has a huge number of lines of code and many different methods. It is usually easier for a developer to add a feature to an existing class than to create a new one, which is why the class grows and too much functionality is crammed into it.

questions.q: Which rule of thumb signals that a method should be split?
o: If a method is called from more than one place, split it
If a method has more than two parameters, split it
If a method contains any loop, split it
If you feel like adding a comment when writing a method, put that functionality in a separate method
questions.e: Two rules apply to a long method: if you feel like adding a comment when writing it, put that functionality in a separate method; and if a method takes more than 10 to 15 lines of code, identify its tasks and subtasks and move the subtasks into separate methods.

questions.q: Beyond how many lines of code should a method's tasks and subtasks be identified and moved into separate methods?
o: 20 to 30 lines
50 lines
5 to 10 lines
10 to 15 lines
questions.e: If a method takes more than 10 to 15 lines of code, identify the tasks and subtasks it performs and try to put the subtasks into separate methods.

questions.q: If local variables prevent part of a long method's functionality from being moved out, the suggested remedy is to:
o: move the entire object to another method
duplicate the method and delete the unused half
delete the local variables
convert the local variables into public fields
questions.e: Ways to eliminate a long method are to move part of the method's functionality into a separate method and, if local variables prevent that, to move the entire object to another method.

questions.q: The smell of using a lot of primitive data types typically arises when:
o: a method returns a primitive rather than an object
the number of fields in a class grows over time and values like currency, dates and phone numbers are stored in primitives or constants instead of small objects
the compiler cannot infer the types of local variables
a class uses object types where primitives would suffice
questions.e: This problem typically occurs when the number of fields in a class grows over time, for example storing currency, date and phone numbers in primitive types or constants instead of small objects.

questions.q: The smell 'too many parameters' occurs if a method:
o: has too much functionality, or implements multiple algorithms
returns more than one value
is called recursively
has fewer parameters than it has local variables
questions.e: Too many parameters occurs if a method has too much functionality or implements multiple algorithms; long parameter lists are difficult to understand and inconvenient to use.

questions.q: What is the suggested remedy for a long parameter list?
o: Add default values so fewer arguments are supplied
Convert the method to a constructor
Replace the parameters with public fields
Pass an entire object instead
questions.e: It is better to pass an entire object. If an object does not have enough data, use a more general object or divide up the method's functionality so each method processes logically related data.

questions.q: A set of logically related fields such as a URL, username, password and schema name is an instance of which smell, and which refactoring addresses it?
o: Temporary field, addressed by inlining
Long method, addressed by extract method
Groups of data, addressed by extract class
Lazy class, addressed by deleting the class
questions.e: Groups of logically related data, such as database connection parameters, should be moved to a separate class; the technique is extract class.

questions.q: Why are public data members considered always a bad idea?
o: They prevent the class from having methods
They cannot be given meaningful names
They make field access slower at runtime
They blur the line between interface and implementation, violate encapsulation and limit future flexibility
questions.e: Public data members blur the line between interface and implementation, inherently violate encapsulation and limit future flexibility; public data members should be hidden behind access routines.

questions.q: If most of the code in a class simply passes calls off to routines in other classes, the suggested action is to:
o: move the other classes into the middleman
eliminate the middleman and call those other classes directly
make the middleman class abstract
add more methods to the middleman class
questions.e: A middleman object that isn't doing anything should be considered for elimination so that the other classes are called directly.

questions.q: The smell 'alternative classes with different interfaces' describes:
o: an interface that no class implements
one class with two constructors of different signatures
multiple classes that do the same thing but whose methods have different names
a class that implements two unrelated interfaces
questions.e: Alternative classes with different interfaces means multiple classes do the same thing, but their methods have different names.

questions.q: The 'temporary field' smell describes a field that:
o: holds a value copied from another class
is declared inside a method rather than the class
an object needs only occasionally and that is empty or null the rest of the time
changes value on every method call
questions.e: If a class has a temporary field that an object needs only occasionally when its value is set, and which is empty or null the rest of the time, the code smells; it is a questionable design decision.

questions.q: If a subclass uses only a small subset of the parent class's functions, this smells of:
o: a missing interface on the parent class
insufficient encapsulation in the parent class
the wrong hierarchy, since inheritance implies the child uses nearly all of the parent's functionality
excessive cohesion in the subclass
questions.e: A subclass using only a small subset of the parent's functions smells of the wrong hierarchy; usually the superfluous methods are simply not overridden or they throw exceptions. One class inheriting another implies the child uses nearly all of the parent's functionality.

questions.q: Code that is never executed is known as:
o: latent code
dead code
orphan code
idle code
questions.e: Superfluous code may take the form of dead code, code that has no effect, and unused values in program logic; code that is never executed is known as dead code.

questions.q: What can most modern compilers do about statements or expressions that have no effect?
o: Nothing, since they cannot be detected
Remove them and silently fix the logic
Convert them into comments
Warn about them
questions.e: Statements or expressions that have no effect should be identified and removed from code; most modern compilers can warn about code that has no effect.

questions.q: Remediating dead code requires the programmer to determine:
o: only how much execution time it would have consumed
not only why the code is never executed, but also whether it should have been executed
only the line number at which the code appears
only whether the compiler warns about it
questions.e: Remediation of dead code requires the programmer to determine not only why the code is never executed but also whether the code should have been executed, and then to resolve that situation appropriately.

questions.q: Consider code in which a variable x can only be assigned a nonzero value along a path that ends with a return statement, and a later 'if (x != 0)' test follows. What is true of that test?
o: Its condition will always evaluate to true
Its condition will never evaluate to true, making the guarded code dead
It will throw an exception at runtime
It will cause a compile-time error
questions.e: Because the only path on which x becomes nonzero ends in a return, control can never reach the later test with a nonzero x, so the condition never evaluates to true and the body is dead code.

questions.q: Which smell makes modification difficult by requiring that subclassing one class forces the creation of another subclass for a different class?
o: Inappropriate intimacy
Complex tree of modifications
Uniformly distributed dependencies
Parallel inheritance hierarchies
questions.e: The three smells that make modification difficult are parallel inheritance hierarchies, uniformly distributed dependencies, and a complex tree of modifications. Parallel inheritance hierarchies manifest when subclassing a class requires creating another subclass for a different class.

questions.q: Which smell is summarised as 'one change, edits in many classes'?
o: Uniformly distributed dependencies
Lazy class
Complex tree of modifications
Parallel inheritance hierarchies
questions.e: With uniformly distributed dependencies, any modification requires looking for all of a class's uses and making a lot of small changes: one change, edits in many classes. The complex tree of modifications is the opposite, summarised as one class, many changes.

questions.q: Which smell is summarised as 'one class, many changes', where changing one method requires fixing another, then a third, and so on?
o: Complex tree of modifications
Duplicated code
Uniformly distributed dependencies
Parallel inheritance hierarchies
questions.e: A complex tree of modifications is the opposite of uniformly distributed dependencies: changes affect a large number of methods in one class, because such code has cascading dependence.

questions.q: A method with a lot of explanatory comments on almost every line is best addressed by:
o: converting the comments into log statements
removing all the comments and leaving the method as it is
splitting the code into several smaller methods with explanatory names
moving the method into a new class of its own
questions.e: A large number of comments in a method usually arises from a complex algorithm, so it is better to split the code into several smaller methods and give them explanatory names.

questions.q: A class that takes on very little functionality although it was planned to be large is called:
o: a lazy class
a middleman
a temporary class
a task-dealer class
questions.e: A lazy class takes on very little functionality though it was planned to be large. A task-dealer class, by contrast, exists only to send a task to another class.

questions.q: A class whose only purpose is to send a task to another class is called:
o: a lazy class
an external method
a parallel hierarchy
a task-dealer class
questions.e: A task-dealer class is needed only for sending a task to another class, which raises the question of whether it should be removed.

questions.q: The smell 'external methods' describes a method that:
o: overrides a method of its superclass
is called only from outside its own package
is declared in an interface rather than a class
uses data from another object much more often than its own data
questions.e: An external method uses data from another object much more often than its own data. It belongs to the category of excessive connectivity, which is characterised by a large number of unjustified relationships in the code.

questions.q: 'Inappropriate intimacy' as a code smell means that:
o: a method is called more often than expected
two classes have identical public interfaces
a class has too many public methods
a class depends on the implementation details of another class
questions.e: Inappropriate intimacy means a class depends on the implementation details of another class; it is one of the excessive connectivity smells.

questions.q: When one class calls another, which requests data from a third, which gets data from a fourth, the resulting smell indicates:
o: high dependence on the current class structure
excessive duplication of code
insufficient use of inheritance
a missing interface definition
questions.e: Such a long chain of calls means high dependence on the current class structure; it is one of the excessive connectivity smells.

questions.q: Which refactoring technique is most appropriate for a long, complex method that performs multiple responsibilities?
o: Remove magic numbers
Extract method
Rename variables and methods
Extract class
questions.e: The extract method technique is useful for a long complex method with multiple responsibilities: extracting tasks into separate methods makes the original less complex and more readable, and the code more reusable and maintainable.

questions.q: An order-processing class that computes a subtotal, a tax rate and a total in one method is improved by extracting which methods?
o: calculateSubtotal, calculateTax and calculateTotalCost
a single calculateAll method
getSubtotal, getTax and getTotal only
processOrder and validateOrder
questions.e: Extracting the subtotal, tax and total logic into calculateSubtotal, calculateTax and calculateTotalCost makes the class more readable, modular and reusable.

questions.q: A Person class holding name, age, street, city, state and zipCode is best refactored by:
o: replacing the address fields with a single string
extracting a separate Address class to hold the address fields and the associated behaviour
making all the address fields public
moving the Person fields into the Address class
questions.e: When a class performs too many functions, some must be moved elsewhere. It is good practice to put the address information and its associated data-processing behaviour into a separate Address class, leaving Person with name, age and an Address reference.

questions.q: Values hardcoded directly into code are called magic numbers and strings. Why are they a problem?
o: They prevent the code from compiling
They always slow the program down at runtime
They make the code less maintainable and increase inconsistencies and errors due to mistypes
They cannot be used inside conditional statements
questions.e: Magic numbers and strings make code less maintainable and increase inconsistencies and errors due to mistypes; the remedy is to refactor to constants with descriptive names.

questions.q: Which declaration correctly replaces a hardcoded database username with a named constant?
o: public static String dbUsername = "user";
private String DB_USERNAME = "user";
private static final String DB_USERNAME = "user";
final DB_USERNAME = "user";
questions.e: Replacing a magic string means introducing a constant with a descriptive name, declared static final so it cannot be reassigned.

questions.q: Duplicate code is dreaded in software development because it:
o: makes classes more cohesive
always increases execution time
increases bug intensity and inconsistencies and bloats the size of the codebase
prevents the use of version control
questions.e: Duplicate code has negative effects on quality, maintainability and efficiency; it increases bug intensity, increases inconsistencies and bloats the size of the codebase.

questions.q: If calculateTotal and calculateAverage both contain the same summing logic, the appropriate refactoring is to:
o: extract the summing logic into a calculateSum method used by both
duplicate the logic into a third method for clarity
move both methods into a superclass without changing them
merge calculateTotal and calculateAverage into one method
questions.e: Extracting the duplicate logic for summing the numbers into a calculateSum method, then having both calculateTotal and calculateAverage use it, removes the duplication.

questions.q: Which step is part of simplifying an overly complex method?
o: Limit the level of nesting within the method
Increase the number of parameters it accepts
Inline all the methods that it calls
Convert the method into a constructor
questions.e: Simplifying a method involves applying the Single Responsibility Principle to it, extracting sub-methods into standalone methods, eliminating redundant and unused code, and limiting the level of nesting within the method.

questions.q: Which principle is applied to a method when simplifying it?
o: The Open-Closed Principle
The Dependency Inversion Principle
The Liskov Substitution Principle
The Single Responsibility Principle
questions.e: The Single Responsibility Principle is applied to the method, alongside extracting sub-methods, eliminating redundant and unused code, and limiting nesting. Note that this principle is sometimes written 'SPR' by mistake; the conventional abbreviation is SRP.

questions.q: Why should the code be understood thoroughly before refactoring it?
o: Because refactoring cannot be reverted once begun
Understanding its functionality, interactions and dependencies guides decisions and avoids changes that affect behaviour
Because refactoring tools require a written summary first
Because understanding the code removes the need for tests
questions.e: Before refactoring a piece of code, ensure you understand its functionality, interactions and dependencies; this comprehension guides decisions and helps avoid changes that may affect the functionality.

questions.q: Breaking a large refactoring into smaller manageable steps achieves what?
o: It removes the need for version control
It eliminates the need for peer review
It reduces the risk of errors and lets changes be validated continuously and easily
It guarantees a performance improvement
questions.e: Breaking the refactoring process into smaller manageable steps makes the workload easier, reduces the risk of errors, and allows changes to be validated continuously and easily.

questions.q: Which version control system allows different software versions to be managed concurrently, so a working backup branch can be kept?
o: Mercurial
Git
Subversion
Perforce
questions.e: Version control systems like Git allow you to manage different software versions concurrently; backing up working software in a separate branch avoids wasting time when a change breaks the software.

questions.q: What role does a suite of tests play before significant refactoring begins?
o: It documents the intended new behaviour
It provides a safety net, validating that the code behaves as expected and that existing functionality remains intact
It measures the performance gain from refactoring
It replaces the need to understand the code
questions.e: Before embarking on significant code changes, especially refactoring, having a suite of tests in place provides a safety net; the tests validate that the code behaves as expected and that existing functionality remains intact.

questions.q: Which modern IDEs provide robust refactoring capabilities such as safe delete, extract method and inline refactoring?
o: Vim and Emacs
BlueJ and NetBeans
Eclipse and IntelliJ
Visual Studio and Xcode
questions.e: With modern IDEs like Eclipse and IntelliJ, refactoring need not be stressful; IntelliJ's features include safe delete, extract method, parameter, field and variable, inline refactoring, and copy and move.

questions.q: What does a complete unit test suite allow a developer to do during refactoring?
o: Avoid documenting the refactoring changes
Skip the need for regression testing afterwards
Detect regressions, ensure functionality is not broken, facilitate collaboration and ensure long-term maintainability
Measure the cyclomatic complexity of each method
questions.e: A complete unit test suite allows you to detect regressions, ensure functionality is not broken, facilitate collaboration and ensure long-term maintainability.

questions.q: Why track performance metrics while refactoring?
o: Because refactoring always degrades performance
To decide which developer should perform the refactoring
Because performance is the only measure of code quality
To validate that refactoring efforts are yielding results and to compare different refactoring strategies
questions.e: Refactoring is not just about improving structure but also performance. Tracking performance metrics takes the guesswork out, validates that efforts are yielding results, and allows different refactoring strategies to be compared.

questions.q: What is the value of a peer review after refactoring changes are made?
o: It makes version control unnecessary
Another developer with a fresh perspective can identify overlooked issues and bring new insights
It replaces the need for regression testing
It guarantees that no bugs were introduced
questions.e: An impartial peer review from a colleague can identify issues you might have overlooked and bring new insights and valuable feedback; it also fosters collaboration and knowledge sharing.

questions.q: Why document refactoring changes when working in a team?
o: Because undocumented changes cannot be committed to version control
Because documentation replaces the need for tests
Because the compiler requires change records
Because the changes may impact colleagues' work, and documentation promotes transparency, knowledge sharing and onboarding
questions.e: Documenting the reasons for changes that may not be immediately obvious promotes collaboration and transparency, and improves knowledge sharing and onboarding.

questions.q: What does regression testing confirm after refactoring is complete?
o: That newly introduced logic does not conflict with the existing code and existing functionality is preserved
That no new classes were created
That the refactored code runs faster than before
That the code conforms to the house style guide
questions.e: Once refactoring is finished, regression testing ensures existing functionalities are preserved and that newly introduced logic does not conflict with the existing code.

questions.q: What is the recommended response to unexpected issues encountered during refactoring?
o: Press on until the refactoring is complete, then debug
Disable the failing tests and continue
Delete the affected class and rewrite it from scratch
Do not hesitate to revert to a working state
questions.e: If unexpected issues arise during refactoring, do not hesitate to revert to a working state; it is better to take a step back than to waste time and resources.

questions.q: Choosing meaningful variable and method names is described as key to making code more:
o: compact
efficient
readable
portable
questions.e: Renaming variables and methods is a refactoring technique: choosing meaningful variable and method names is key to making code more readable.

questions.q: Ordering tests by frequency is a code tuning technique in which conditional checks or branches are organised:
o: based on their likelihood of occurrence, with the most frequent case tested first
from the most expensive condition to the cheapest
in the order in which they were originally written
in alphabetical order of the variables tested
questions.e: Ordering tests by frequency organises conditional checks or branches based on their likelihood of occurrence, so the most frequent case is tested first.

questions.q: What benefit does ordering tests by frequency provide?
o: It minimizes unnecessary comparisons, improving performance in frequently executed sections
It reduces the amount of memory the program needs
It makes the conditions easier to read aloud
It removes the need for an else branch
questions.e: Ordering tests by frequency helps minimize unnecessary comparisons, improving performance especially in frequently executed sections of code.

questions.q: Ordering tests by frequency applies to which constructs?
o: while loops only
if-else statements only
switch statements only
Both if-else statements and switch statements
questions.e: In if-else statements, conditions are reordered so the most frequent case is tested first; in switch statements, the cases are reordered so the most frequent case comes first.

questions.q: Table lookup, also known as a lookup table or array lookup, speeds up a program by:
o: compressing data so less memory is read
reordering conditional tests by frequency
expanding a loop body so fewer iterations run
